newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Mitterrand aide kept classified files.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Mitterrand aide kept classified files.

text.p: The former head of French ex-President Francois Mitterrand's anti-terrorist unit said on Friday he had held on to the group's files after it was disbanded to prevent them being stolen.
DST counter-espionage officers and two investigating magistrates probing a telephone bugging scandal seized the archives last week at a garage outside Paris rented by Christian Prouteau.

The files also included recordings linked to the investigation and were found days ahead of a Supreme Court ruling due on March 4 on whether to stop the probe into alleged illegal phone-tapping by the unit at the Elysee presidential palace.

"It's because I no longer have an office at the Elysee since the election of (Jacques) Chirac in May 1995 that I put these dossiers in a safe place to prevent anyone stealing them," Prouteau told the newspaper Liberation.

"The Interior Ministry never asked me for my files, otherwise I would have handed them to the authorities," added Prouteau, who along with two former senior government officials and three members of the since-disbanded unit has been placed under investigation.

The unit allegedly tapped the phones of dozens of politicians, lawyers, and journalists without the required judicial permission. Among those being investigated are Mitterrand's former chief of staff Gilles Menage.

Liberation reported that the files included explosive notes from the DST and from the DGSE military secret service, classified alphabetically under A for "Abu Nidal", I for "Ireland", "IRA", or G for "Greenpeace" among others.

"If I had handed these documents to state archives in 1995, it would have taken 50 years to get them out again. I was convinced I would be appointed to another job, and that the dossiers on terrorist groups could be useful to me," Prouteau said.
He denied that he had stolen or violated state secrets. "My life is ruined. You think it's fun to be always compared to the Stasi?" he said, a reference to the secret police of former East Germany.

Louis Schweitzer, the chairman of carmaker Renault, who was at the time chief aide to then prime minister Laurent Fabius, and former labour minister Michel Delebarre, who was chief aide to then prime minister Pierre Mauroy, are also being probed.
